entries.title: Natasha Cloud calls Enes Kanter Freedom "irrelevant," redirects focus to issues affecting women
entries.summary: <p>NEW YORK—Speaking to reporters for the first time since her confrontation with provocateur <b>Enes Kanter Freedom</b>, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky</a> guard <b>Natasha Cloud</b> declined to give him any more attention.</p><p>“I’m not going to address an irrelevant person,” Cloud said.</p><p>Instead, Cloud used the question to draw attention to issues she believes have far greater consequences for women and children, including domestic violence, sexual assault, food insecurity, access to health care and mortality among women.</p><p>Cloud said she believes the right wing in the United States is using the WNBA as a pawn to distract from those issues ahead of the midterm elections.</p><p>“It is an intentional distraction,” Cloud said. “The more that we hate each other and have bias against each other, the more we’re going to be distracted from real-life issues that are plaguing these communities that we’re here to support and here to protect."</p><p>Cloud also pointed to the hypocrisy of right-wing commentators who now say the WNBA and its players need to be protected.</p><p>“Y’all were the same ones saying that we shouldn’t be paid,” Cloud said. “Y’all were the same ones saying that we’re a joke. Y’all are the same ones that don’t respect Black women. If you’re going to protect women, that means all women. That means Black women, trans women, and the list goes on and on.”</p><p>Kanter Freedom, who recently claimed to be a woman and declared for the WNBA draft, was ejected from a recent Sky-Fever game after getting into a verbal altercation with Cloud. The Sky later banned him from attending their games, with principal owner Michael Alter saying Kanter Freedom would not be welcomed back unless he could prove to the organization that he would abide by its rules.</p><p>Cloud said she feels fully supported by the Sky, including Alter, general manager <b>Jeff Pagliocca</b> and coach <b>Tyler Marsh.</b></p><p>“Michael goes and bans [Kanter Freedom],” Cloud said. “That’s immediate action. We’re asking for protection. That’s what protection looks like from a man.</p><p>“We can’t not allow him in the arena before the game, but after the game, we can bring solutions to the table that benefit putting our players first. I think that Jeff, Tyler and Michael have done a really good job of that.”</p><p>Cloud is one of the league's most vocal players on social and political issues. But she pushed back against the notion that she enjoys being at the center of such conversations.</p><p>“None of this is performative,” Cloud said. “I don’t want to put myself in front of fires all the time. I don’t want to be the one that always has to speak up, but somebody has to [expletive] do it.”</p><p>She said remaining silent would be a disservice to the communities she cares about and identifies with, particularly when she has a platform capable of drawing attention to the issues affecting them.</p><p>At the same time, Cloud lamented that controversies such as the one involving Kanter Freedom tend to overshadow every other aspect of the league.</p><p>“I would love for our league to be celebrated for the amazing year that we’re having,” Cloud said. “Our transformative CBA, our viewership going through the roof — you have so many players playing at such an elite level, but we don’t even talk about it because we are a microcosm of a bigger issue in our society.”</p>

entries.title: Market eyes August jobs report after unexpected employment stall in July
entries.summary: <p>NEW YORK (AP) — Wall Street will get several important updates this week about the health of the U.S. jobs market.</p><p>On Tuesday, the U.S. will release its July report focusing on job openings and turnover. It provides details on job openings within specific industries and areas of the economy. It also provides details on turnover, including layoffs and people quitting their jobs.</p><p>The government will release a broader and closely-watched monthly employment report on Friday. The monthly jobs report for August will provide details on job growth and unemployment for a wide range of industries, along with public sector employment.</p><p>The employment report for July showed that the U.S. job market stalled unexpectedly. Employment has been a mostly resilient area of the economy even as stubborn inflation continues to squeeze businesses and households, while consumer confidence weakens.</p><p>A weakening employment market could create a tough situation for Federal Reserve. The central bank has to balance fighting inflation with supporting employment and its main tool for that “dual mandate” remains interest rates. Raising its benchmark rate to fight stubbornly high inflation could further damage the jobs market. Cutting its benchmark interest rate to help support employment could worsen inflation.</p><p>The Fed has been holding rates steady as it monitors the impact on inflation from the U.S. war with Iran, which has raised crude oil prices, making everything from gasoline to shipped products more expensive. That is on top of an ongoing U.S. trade war with much of the world that has made many goods more expensive.</p>

entries.title: Andrew Benintendi’s bat, experience coming in clutch for first-place White Sox
entries.summary: <p>MINNEAPOLIS — Designated hitter Andrew Benintendi hasn’t skipped a beat since returning to the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" target="_blank" ><u>White Sox</u></a>’ batting order this weekend, going 2-for-4 with a double and two RBI in the series opener.</p><p>His RBI single and solo home run made the difference in a 3-2 victory on Saturday, adding a double and scoring another run on a 3-for-4 afternoon at the plate.</p><p>Benintendi’s 34 hits with runners in scoring position this season put him in the top 10 among American League DHs, while his <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/07/22/andrew-benintendi-white-sox" target="_blank" ><u>quiet production</u></a> (.751 OPS with 14 homers) has made him a stalwart for manager Will Venable.</p><p>“Every one of our guys can learn from Benny and how he approaches it with runners in scoring position,” Venable said. “It's about his experience. It's about his understanding of his own strengths. And he's been on the field in every type of situation that there is.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Benny puts one on the board! 💥 <a href="https://t.co/kLG7pqzDmt">pic.twitter.com/kLG7pqzDmt</a></p>— Chicago White Sox (@whitesox) <a href="https://x.com/whitesox/status/2093787598695039250?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">August 29, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p></p><h3><b>Rivalry rekindled?</b></h3><p>Veteran Twins starter Joe Ryan has seen several iterations of the division-rival White Sox over his six-year career — most of them bad. He’s as surprised as anyone by a squad aiming to bury Minnesota in the standings.</p><p>“That's been a crazy revamp,” said Ryan, who’s on the mend with a glute strain. “You can just see the energy on the field. It’s so different there.</p><p>“In the past, it was kind of like, you’ve still got to pitch well, but they didn't seem like they really always wanted to be there,” Ryan said. “Now it just seems like they're hungry for it.”</p><h3><b>HR streak peters out</b></h3><p>Center fielder Tristan Peters’ franchise-record-tying, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/08/26/tristan-peters-white-sox-munetaka-murakami-colson-montgomery-franchise-record-frank-thomas-paul-konerko-carlos-lee-will-venable" target="_blank" ><u>five-game home run streak</u></a> ended Friday, but the All-Star rookie still got a hit in the series opener and scored from third on a passed ball.</p><p>It was just the latest feat in a stunning year for the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/07/18/tristan-peters-white-sox-all-star-toronto-canada" target="_blank" ><u>Manitoba-born</u></a> former Savannah Banana who played at Southern Illinois University long before the Sox acquired him for peanuts last offseason.</p><p>Peters goes down as the only player in MLB history to hit for the cycle, hit a grand slam and walkoff bomb, homer in five straight, notch a six-RBI game and reach base safely five times in a game all in one season, per STATS.</p><h3><b>Murakami flashes leather</b></h3><p>Rookie sensation Munetaka Murakami entered play Saturday hitting a paltry .148/.313/.352 over his previous 15 games, but he’s finding other ways to contribute.</p><p>The first baseman turned a nifty, inning-ending double play with runners on the corners, vacuuming up a grounder from the Twins’ Luke Keaschall, stepping on the bag and throwing a dart to catcher Drew Romo to nab Trevor Larnach at the plate.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">GOT 'EM! <a href="https://t.co/JSKbkwKG65">pic.twitter.com/JSKbkwKG65</a></p>— Chicago White Sox (@whitesox) <a href="https://x.com/whitesox/status/2093526789784006837?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">August 29, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Venable said Murakami arrived with plenty of natural instinct from our years in Japan as a third baseman, “but there's a lot of nuance in that position and a lot of subtle details that Mune's doing a really good job of learning and growing on… It's been cool to watch him develop over there.”</p><h3><b>Drafted to sing</b></h3><p>Romo’s teammates tasked him with singing the national anthem before kicking off their fantasy football draft at a Minneapolis hotel.</p><p>Video evidence shared on social media by Erick Fedde suggests the Sox don’t have to worry about losing their backup backstop to the music industry.</p><p>“They played a longer, slower version by Chris Stapleton, and he's extremely hard to compete with,” Romo explained.</p><p>Reliever Sean Newcomb selected Detroit running back Jahmyr Gibbs with the first pick.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Drew Romo and Kenzo Yagi open the White Sox fantasy draft with moving renditions of the anthem 🫡<br><br>(via erickfedde • IG) <a href="https://t.co/oYIvMnkn13">pic.twitter.com/oYIvMnkn13</a></p>— Sox On 35th (@SoxOn35th) <a href="https://x.com/SoxOn35th/status/2093171904114770074?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">August 28, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p></p>

entries.title: Grant Taylor flexing his muscle for a flexible White Sox bullpen
entries.summary: <p>MINNEAPOLIS — It’s a “day-to-day operation” down the home stretch for <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" target="_blank" ><u>White Sox</u></a> manager Will Venable and his beleaguered pitching staff.</p><p>Down a pair of starters and dealing with inconsistency from the rest of the rotation, Venable said he couldn’t even sketch out his plan on the mound for Sunday’s series finale in Minneapolis until he saw how things played out Saturday.</p><p>The late-summer pitching triage situation has underscored the value of powerhouse reliever Grant Taylor, who turned in his longest outing of the season Friday when the Sox needed it most in a divisional showdown.</p><p>“He's just pounding the zone,” said Venable, who called in the second-year right hander in the sixth inning Friday to escape a one-out, two-on jam before sailing through two more innings on a total of 27 pitches with three punchouts.</p><p>“That's a big ask, but he's just so efficient,” Venable said. “It obviously saved the day for us there.”</p><p>Not that anyone in the organization is all that worried who’s in line for the save. The Sox deployed Taylor as an opener four times over the first month of the season but have reserved his 98 mph fastball and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/06/28/grant-taylor-white-sox-bullpen-jacob-gonzalez-walkoff-jaden-fauske" target="_blank" ><u>knee-buckling curve</u></a> for high-leverage situations against opposing teams’ best hitters anytime from the sixth inning on.</p><p>Taylor, who lowered his ERA to 2.03 over 52 outings with 92 strikeouts in 71 innings, had pushed for a rotation spot before the season, but he’s enjoying his ride as Venable’s designated shutdown man.</p><p>“The buildup has been pretty solid,” said Taylor, a 2023 second-round draft pick out of LSU. “Started the year with a lot of ones, mixed in some twos for a while. So the third up, I might be a little more tired the next day, but it’s just kind of part of the deal now.</p><p>“We’re in a tight game, and I’m called upon and I’m ready for it,” he said.</p><p>That’s the attitude across a relief corps that has hit some speed bumps in the second half but stood tall behind Taylor, a resurgent <a class="Link" entries.summary: <p>NEW YORK — Sydney Taylor was talking to herself during a dead ball.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky</a> rookie practiced the motion of her jumper, then replayed the dribble move she had just made. The open pull-up had rattled around the rim. Another shot slightly off.</p><p>It has been that kind of stretch for Taylor, who's shooting 30.2% from the field and 25% from three-point range in the last four games. She finished the Sky’s blowout loss to the Liberty on Saturday with 13 points on 4-for-14 shooting.</p><p>It is the first real slump for Taylor since she burst onto the scene in June and established herself not only as the Sky’s best shot-creator, but as one of the best rookies in her class.</p><p>A groin injury disrupted her rhythm. Taylor has been on a roughly 20-minute restriction since returning, a difficult adjustment for a volume scorer. Groin injuries also are notoriously difficult to recover from.</p><p>“Just trying to fight through it,” Taylor said after the game. “Keep playing. I know my teammates need me to do a lot more than just scoring the ball, so next-play mentality.”</p><p>Taylor is clearly frustrated, struggling individually as the Sky have lost three straight and been eliminated from playoff contention. But coach Tyler Marsh sees value in what she is experiencing.</p><p>“It’s going to help continue to mold her into who she’s going to be in this league,” he said before the game. “It’s not always going to be sunshine and rainbows for you. As a top-tier scorer, she’s got to continue to find ways to battle through adversity and nights where it’s not going her way. You can tell she’s been frustrated the last two with shots not falling.”</p><p>The key for Taylor, as Marsh has emphasized throughout the season, is not falling in love with her three-pointer. He wants her to get a few looks near the basket first, then allow those opportunities to open up her outside game.</p><p>Her most difficult-to-guard attribute, at least right now, is her lightning speed. Defenders struggle to keep her in front, and she has a soft touch around the basket.</p><p>Taylor leaned on that speed at times Saturday, reaching the paint with a few ankle-breaking moves and getting to the free-throw line. But even there, she made only three of six attempts.</p><p>“Any time she comes to me, I meet her with a smile because it’s like, look: This is what you wanted, this is what you got,” Marsh said. “This is part of being a great player. She’s going to have more nights like that, but she’s also going to have more nights where she’s in the 20, 25, 30 range, where she’s hitting game-winners.”</p><p>Taylor was far from the only player who struggled to score Saturday, as both teams shot below 40%. But the Liberty made 11 three-pointers to the Sky’s four and converted their free throws.</p><p>The Sky now enter the FIBA break, which runs from Aug. 31 through Sept. 16, with four games left and no playoff race to motivate them.</p><p>Marsh wants to use the remaining games to build for the future, giving younger players more minutes while being mindful of the wear on those who have carried heavier workloads. But maintaining urgency can be difficult once the season’s central goal is gone.</p><p>Maybe the break can provide the reset both Taylor and the Sky need.</p><p>“I think it’s important mentally, emotionally and physically to just kind of recoup, so they’re coming back for the last few games of the season with a clear mind and a new vision for how we want to end the season,” Marsh said. “Sometimes you need to get away and latch onto some things that mean just as much as basketball. Be with loved ones and enjoy the time to yourself. I think that’s very important.”</p>

entries.title: Sammy Sosa basking in rebuilt relationship with Cubs
entries.summary: <p>Life seems to be good for <b>Sammy Sosa</b>. He plays a lot of golf, travels and is firmly back in the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs’</a> good graces.</p><p>“It’s like a marriage: sometimes in the marriage you get mad [at] your wife but you come back and love her,” Sosa said of his relationship with the Cubs. “You put everything behind and move forward.</p><p>“I feel that the way they treated me… I’m glad that we [came] to that conclusion and stayed together and pretty much put our differences [to] the side. Right now, we’re happy.”</p><p>For 13 seasons, Sosa and the Cubs were synonymous. In 1993, he became the team’s first player to steal 30 bases and hit 30 home runs in the same season. He exploded to international superstardom in 1998 thanks to his home run race with <b>Mark McGwire</b> and led the Cubs to the National League Wild Card, earning league MVP honors. Five years later, Sosa hit two home runs and batted .308 against the Marlins in the 2003 NLCS, coming within a game of making the World Series.</p><p>Then everything came apart at the end of a toxic 2004 season when Sosa left the final game of the year early. Sosa, in decline from his 60-homer days and plagued with speculation around performance enhancing drugs, was traded to the Orioles in January 2005.</p><p>The two sides were estranged until Dec. 2024 when Sosa released a statement to apologize for past mistakes but didn’t specify what the errors were. Regardless, he and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2024/12/19/sammy-sosa-and-cubs-begin-reconciliation" >Cubs ownership reconciled</a>, Sosa was subsequently invited to the 2025 Cubs Convention and inducted into the team’s Hall of Fame.</p><p>On Saturday, he was part of the celebration of the Cubs’ 150th National League anniversary. Introduced to the crowd before the game with a group that included 2016 champions and Hall of Famers, Sosa received one of the loudest ovations.</p><p>“I’m grateful to be among some of the legends that played before me,” Sosa said. “I’m happy with that.”</p><h2><b>Eyes on the prize</b></h2><p>Even with <b>Dansby Swanson </b>(left oblique strain) on the injured list, the Cubs are not lacking depth. Depending on the scenario, they can throw in <b>Matt Shaw</b>, <b>Michael Conforto </b>or <b>Tyrone Taylor </b>and still get production from dependable major-league players.</p><p>Cubs manager <b>Craig Counsell </b>said he feels “pretty good” that he has all situations in a game covered, but knows certain ones matter more than others.</p><p>“We’ve got to win the big situations,” Counsell said.</p><h2>Injury updates</h2><p>Swanson<b> </b>will begin swinging a bat again soon. Counsell said “that starts the challenging part” of Swanson’s recovery because it requires bodily rotation and the kind of movement that put him on the shelf.</p><p>“The fact that he’s even on the field doing athletic things is a really good sign,” Counsell said.</p><p>Swanson was put on the IL on Aug. 17, a day after getting hurt on an awkward swing during a loss to the Cardinals.</p><p><b>Edward Cabrera </b>(right middle finger blister) will be going to Triple-A Iowa this week for a rehab assignment. Like Swanson, Cabrera’s injury happened Aug. 16 when a blister developed on his finger during his start against St. Louis.</p>

entries.title: QB Tyson Bagent, 3 rookies pace Bears vs Titans
entries.summary: <p>NASHVILLE, Tenn. — Tyson Bagent recognized man coverage, and a pending blitz, and took the snap. The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a>’ backup quarterback backpedaled into his own end zone, watched running back Roschon Johnson block the blitzer and launched what would be the easiest pass he threw all Saturday night.</p><p>Rookie receiver Zavion Thomas ran a double move route down the right sideline. When he stutter-stepped, cornerback Keydrain Calligan was caught so off-balanced that he fell to the ground when he turned to keep running. Thomas caught the ball a full seven yards behind Calligan and sprinted for a 97-yard touchdown.</p><p>There was no way he’d be caught — the Bears’ third-round pick ran a 4.28-second 40-yard dash at the NFL Scouting Combine, the third-fastest among all prospects.</p><p>The Bears’ first offensive play on Saturday night’s game against the Titans set the tone the Bears wanted from the few players they might need to rely on during the regular season. They led 14-9 at halftime.</p><p>They already know what they have in Bagent, whom coach Ben Johnson considers one of the more valuable players inside Halas Hall despite the fact that Caleb Williams has stayed healthy since he was picked No. 1 overall two years ago.</p><p>To see Bagent look like the preseason monster of previous years, though, was a good reminder to the Bears — and the rest of the league — about what he could do. With Caleb Williams He was almost perfect in his one half’s worth of work, going 16-for-17 for 208 yards and two touchdown passes. He went into the locker room as the team’s leading rusher, too, after running twice for 21 yards.</p><p>Three Bears rookies were just as encouraging.</p><p>In the first half alone, Thomas caught three passes for 116 yards, returned a punt for 39 yards and a kickoff for 22. He flashed the speed that enticed the Bears to take him with the 25<sup>th</sup> pick of the third round despite the fact that he lacked impressive receiving stats at LSU. The Bears sold him as a return wiz who could give coach Ben Johnson a new offensive weapon with which to play. He was exactly that Saturday night, even with the caveat that he was going up against backups. Calligan, for example, is a second-year former undrafted free agent.</p><p>Thomas’ first half had one glaring flaw, though — he fumbled a fly sweep handoff from Bagent toward the end of the first quarter. The Titans recovered and eventually kicked a 56-yard field goal.</p><p>Thomas outperformed No. 4 overall pick Carnell Tate. The Chicago native thought he was open for a 48-yard touchdown pass at the end of the Titans’ first drive before safety Dillon Thieneman, the Bears’ own first-round pick, broke up Will Levis’ pass in the end zone.</p><p>A third Bears rookie contributed, too. When Johnson decided to go for it on fourth-and-1 from his own 21 halfway through the second quarter, Bagent faked a handoff rolled right and threw to third-round pick Sam Roush. The third-round tight end gained 19 yards for a first down.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/08/29/bears-titans-caleb-williams-most-starters-not-playing-preseason-finale-nashville-tyson-bagent-nfl" target="_blank" >Williams and most of the Bears starters</a> — all but Thieneman and linebacker T.J. Edwards, who played two series — could only smile. Williams went through an extensive warmup with his teammates hours before kickoff and watched from the sideline in a gray T-shirt and sunglasses. A little less than half the Bears' 90-man roster sat out.</p><p>The Titans, who said Thursday they'd play their starters, wound up sitting most of them, including former No. 1 overall pick Cam Ward.</p>

entries.title: Bears LB T.J. Edwards rare starter to get snaps in preseason finale vs. Titans
entries.summary: <p>NASHVILLE, Tenn. — The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> sat their starters for the final preseason game against the Titans on Saturday with one surprising exception: Veteran linebacker T.J. Edwards.</p><p>Edwards has had a limited workload in training camp after tweaking his right calf muscle while training in the offseason, and coach Ben Johnson has talked frequently about paying attention to the total number of reps for players. In Edwards’ case, that number would’ve been relatively low going into Saturday.</p><p>Not that he needs the work as he heads into his eighth season, but there was some value in Edwards getting some snaps — he didn’t play in the Bears’ first two preseason games — because he has the in-helmet radio to get play calls from defensive coordinator Dennis Allen.</p><p>Edwards played two series with a unit made up mostly of second-stringers — rookie safety <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/06/11/bears-1st-round-pick-dillion-thieneman-heads-toward-training-camp-with-much-to-learn-earn" >Dillon Thieneman</a> was the only other starter — as the Bears held the Titans’ backups to a three-and-out and a 28-yard field goal by Joey Slye. He led the team with five tackles at that point and headed to the sideline for the rest of the game.</p><p>Edwards has been a crucial piece for the Bears since arriving from the Eagles as a free agent in 2023 and got a contract extension last year that secured him through the ’27 season. He missed time multiple injuries last season, then broke his leg in the playoff win over the Packers.</p><p>The Bears will go into the season with Edwards and newcomer Devin Bush as their starting linebackers with D’Marco Jackson likely next in line. Bush played 24 snaps over the first two preseason games, but didn’t dress Saturday.</p>

entries.summary: <p>St. Rita’s strength this season is a rugged, experienced offensive line. entries.title: Blue-chippers? Bears GM Ryan Poles has compiled solid list going into season, and it could grow
entries.summary: <p>NASHVILLE, Tenn. — Battles for roster spots are one of the more dramatic parts of training camp, and there will be a flurry of activity for <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >the Bears</a> on Sunday as they narrow the team from 90 players to 53 by the 5 p.m. deadline, but the top of the roster matters a lot more than the bottom.</p><p>While there always are players like wide receiver Jahdae Walker, who made the cut last summer and came up big months later with the tying touchdown catch in the final minute against the Packers, the players whose jobs were locked in from the start are the ones who will decide how far the Bears go.</p><p>Most of them didn’t dress for the final preseason game Saturday night against the Titans as Bears coach <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2025/09/01/the-bears-and-their-fans-needed-a-truth-teller-they-got-one-in-new-coach-ben-johnson" >Ben Johnson</a> prioritized health with an eye on the Sept. 13 opener at the Panthers.</p><p>The outlook on the Bears’ top talent was bleak when Ryan Poles came aboard as general manager in 2022, which is why the job was open. Predecessor Ryan Pace left him little upon which to build, and the Bears basically started from scratch.</p><p>Worse than scratch, really, considering Pace also left behind a salary-cap mess and a draft-capital deficit.</p><p>It was silly that the Bears needed former executive Bill Polian to come in and tell them how bad things were, but he made a valid point in saying Pace's roster was light on elite players, or “blue-chippers,” as he called them. He estimated they had 6-8, though realistically the number proved to be half that.</p><p>Pace’s undoing was primarily a combination of striking out at quarterback and failing to stock the roster with young players on a path to stardom.</p><p>Poles is entering a critical phase in evaluating whether Caleb Williams is a franchise quarterback after progress last season but significant steps still ahead. His choices throughout the rest of the lineup, though, have given the Bears a shot to compete.</p><p>Those pieces stand taller on offense, where the Bears jumped from last in the league in 2024 to sixth last season under Johnson, who influenced the acquisitions of several blue-chip pieces.</p><p>The offensive line, long a vulnerability under Pace, has a future Hall of Famer in left guard Joe Thuney and Pro Bowl-caliber players in their 20s in right guard Jonah Jackson and right tackle Darnell Wright.</p><p>Tight end Colston Loveland, the No. 10 overall pick last season, led the team in receptions, yards receiving and touchdown catches as a rookie. He has been an absolute monster in training camp and is a popular pick to be one of the NFL’s best at his position.</p><p>Don’t forget running back D’Andre Swift, either. He was the Bears’ consolation prize when bidding got too high for Saquon Barkley in 2024, but has turned out to be an ideal weapon. He has averaged more than 1,000 yards per season over the last three and is coming off the best performance of his career: 1,087 yards and nine touchdowns.</p><p>Swift has been so good — plus, his role could expand this season — that the Bears could consider a contract extension. He’s entering the final season of a deal that has paid an average of $8 million per season, which ranks 19th at his position.</p><p>Defensively, the Bears know what they have in cornerback Jaylon Johnson and defensive end Montez Sweat. Those are stars any team would want.</p><p>They believe they’ll get that level of play out of rookie safety Dillon Thieneman, a first-rounder who was the second player picked at his position, but draft pedigree doesn’t guarantee anything. The Bears will have to see how much and how quickly he progresses throughout this season.</p><p>They could reasonably classify safety Coby Bryant and nickel cornerback Kyler Gordon as blue-chip players, but they don’t have either of them at the moment. Bryant will miss most or all of this season with a knee injury, and Gordon’s health is a total unknown.</p><p>Gordon missed 14 games last season with three injuries and has been out most of the offseason with a new one. One of the most interesting decisions the Bears actually face is whether to put him on the active roster to start the season.</p><p>The Bears have other players who could move into the blue-chip tier, such as Williams and wide receivers Rome Odunze and Luther Burden, but they need to show indisputable evidence.</p><p>Poles eventually nailed the coaching hire by landing Ben Johnson after three brutal seasons of Matt Eberflus, and a lot of the Bears’ hope in player development hinges on him.</p><p>Is Johnson’s system enough to turn no-names into quality pieces? Is he adept at solving problems on the defensive side even though he’s an offensive-minded coach? Those are questions he’ll have to answer this season.</p><p>But Poles has given him a solid enough place to start, and the Bears have far more GM-coach cohesion than they’ve had in a long time.</p>

entries.title: Chaos meets corruption: Players in NFL camps heading back to college
entries.summary: <p>Let’s just say for 116 years, you devised a system that used and exploited young adults you allowed to play sports for you, using “free” education as collateral for what you received from them in return.</p><p>Then guilt (pressured guilt, but still guilt to a degree) set in, say, 111 years later. And you, a group with a long history of unfair labor and under-compensated practices in sports, began to do (almost) everything you could to right your past wrongs. Let’s call it athletic reparations.</p><p>And that guilt-free system worked in your favor until now. When the chaos finally met and matched the corruption. And the term “amateur status” just turned gray in area.</p><p>A player entered the NFL Draft after four years of playing in the NCAA. During that time, the NCAA instituted a fifth-year option called the 5-in-5 rule, which allowed players who entered college in 2022 to have a fifth year of playing eligibility. The player participated in workouts and camps to make an NFL roster but failed, so he decided (or was told) to exercise that fifth year. He kept his name in the transfer portal and returned to a school of agreed choice between him and head coach. It was OK because it was legal for the player and broke no known NCAA laws. It was above genius.</p><p>The “why,” especially with the ability of NCAA players today to make all that money via NIL, is fully understood. It’s the “how” that seems to have caught even the most profound football and media experts off guard.</p><p>“How” can this happen? How “did” this happen? And how was it “allowed” to happen?</p><p>Who in the “Lane Kiffin” found a loophole in the bylaws of the transition from “amateur” to “professional” athlete, then “training camp back to college” so open that of the two initial players (first Dae’Quan Wright, then Zxavian Harris) who challenged the 5-in-5 rule, both reentered the NCAA and chose to play for the same school, same coach: Kiffin?</p><p>(Note: The infamous and brilliant Drew Rosenhaus just happens to be Wright’s agent.)</p><p>That caused emergency late-night meetings by university athletic directors, presidents and chancellors and the releasing of emergency joint-policy statements. Or as the public discussion was framed: “Big 10, SEC [and other conferences] band together to ban NFL players from returning to play in the NCAA.”</p><p>For players who may not have technically or legally been “NFL” players.</p><p>According to C. Lamont Smith, a longtime NFL agent whose clients included Barry Sanders, Jerome Bettis and Eddie George, not only is the emphasis on the NCAA to clean up this situation, but there needs to be language put in place by the NCAA to define when a player crosses the equator from one phase to the next. From legally non-professional to officially professional.</p><p>“If [the NCAA] really wanted to cover their butts, they’d broaden the language to ‘anyone who pursued or participated in professional football activities,’ and that would cover it all,” Smith said via phone conversation for this column. “I think what you have is a conflict in what the NFL defines as an NFL player and what the NCAA and some of these conferences are describing as an NFL player.”</p><p>Ambiguity at its finest because the NFL collective-bargaining agreement seems to have no clear-cut definition of what exactly a “player” or “NFL player” even is. But that still is not a problem the NFL has to figure out. That all falls on the NCAA as it is the one fighting against non-defined NFL players (a k a: professional football players) with eligibility left from being able to return to familiar workplaces on college campuses for one more year.</p><p>It’s complicated, confusing and (slightly) corrupt. But also not illegal. The goal here is to win games in the NCAA, not, as Mike Greenberg said, “to achieve some state of morality that the sport has absolutely never aspired to.”</p><p>But the internal fight the NCAA is moving toward having with itself has the power to be the final undoing of the system it has been trying to correct for the last five years only to find out that the damage might have been too systemic to repair. The semi-psychokinesis mind games the NCAA played on its prey for all those years has come back to roost, scream, holler, demand and sue.</p><p>Fear of the antitrust lawsuits sitting in wait, waiting by any prosecutor for their phone to ring to prove in court that the NCAA has been unfair to either a singular or multiple want-to-come-back student-athletes will be the NCAA nightmare that keeps on giving.</p><p>In the climate of now that has become college and pro football, if it is more financially beneficial to play in college for a year than it is to keep attempting to be in the NFL — chase that paper until you can legally no longer further your college career and you legally are deemed by the court of law and the laws of the NCAA either a “professional” or an “NFL” (or NBA or WNBA because they were also included in the official argument) player.</p><p>The choice is theirs. Or yours. Until the courts (state, appellate or possibly Supreme), the Senate (or Congress if all decide to get involved) and (not “or”) the NCAA say you no longer have a choice.</p>

entries.title: Chicago State falls to Roosevelt in first football game in school history
entries.summary: <p>Despite a solid start, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/college-sports" target="_blank" >Chicago State</a> — debuting as an independent in the Division I FCS ranks — lost its first football game in school history Saturday, falling to Division II Roosevelt 44-28 at SeatGeek Stadium in Bridgeview.</p><p>Chicago State opened a 7-3 lead after the first quarter, but Roosevelt outscored the Cougars 24-7 in the second quarter and never slipped again.</p><p>Roosevelt quarterback Tony Chachino, formerly of Geneva High School, completed 20 of 32 passes for 236 yards, with three touchdowns and no interceptions. Running back Jaden Bossie, a former Mount Carmel star, rushed for 141 yards and a touchdown in 22 carries. He also caught five passes for 91 yards and another touchdown.</p><p>Chicago State was led by quarterback Ashton Pannell, who’s from Long Beach, California. He completed 29 of 40 passes for 264 yards, with three touchdowns and two interceptions.</p><p>Chicago State has an enrollment of about 2,500, well below the average in the Northeast and across the FCS.</p><p>CSU’s roster includes 20 players from Chicago and five others from Illinois.</p><p>“We’re building it brick-by-brick,” wide receiver Arshawn Powell, who redshirted at Southern Illinois last season, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/college-sports/2026/08/28/chicago-state-university-football-northeast-conference-bobby-rome-fcs-cfb" target="_blank" >told the Sun-Times</a> last week. “It’s not about us. It’s for Chicago.”</p><p>Powell caught five passes for 39 yards and a touchdown.</p>

entries.title: Bears QB Caleb Williams, most starters not playing preseason finale
entries.summary: <p>NASHVILLE, Tenn. — Caleb Williams' exhibition season is over — the Bears quarterback will not play in the team's finale against the Titans on Saturday. </p><p>Tyson Bagent, the second-stringer, went through warmups with the starters. Williams watched from the sideline in a T-shirt and sunglasses.</p><p>Most of the Bears' starters will sit out the game. Williams threw passes to his top receivers hours before kickoff.</p><p>Bears coach Ben Johnson had been noncommittal the past two weeks about whether he'd play his starters following a joint practice. He gave his starting offense nine snaps — two came back because of penalties — two days after practicing against the Bengals last week. He opted against that this week. The team's starters played significant snaps in stifling heat on Thursday at the Titans' practice facility. </p><p>Saturday night's game — the latest preseason finale in the NFL — will be one last chance to Bears players to earn a roster spot. The team must cut its roster down to 53 players by 5 p.m. Sunday.</p>

entries.title: Man, 73, in critical condition after South Shore shooting
entries.summary: <p>A 73-year-old man was in critical condition, and a 23-year-old man was also hospitalized Saturday after they were both shot in South Shore, Chicago police said.</p><p>The men were struck along the 7100 block of South Jeffery Boulevard at about 11:20 a.m., police said.</p><p>The 73-year-old man was found at the scene with a gunshot wound to the buttocks. The 23-year-old man shot transported himself to the University of Chicago Medical Center, police said.</p><p>The older man was also taken to the same hospital, police said.</p><p>Area 1 detectives are investigating.</p>
